plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the double integral of (2x - y^2) over the triangular region R enclosed between y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, and y = 3. The figure shows the triangular region R in the xy-plane with vertices at (-2, 3), (0, 1), and (2, 3); the bounding lines y = 3 (top), y = -x + 1 (lower left), and y = x + 1 (lower right) are labeled. The y-axis divides R into two sub-regions: R1 (shaded blue, left half) and R2 (shaded yellow, right half), each with a red vertical strip indicating the direction of inner integration. The figure illustrates the decomposition of R into two type-I sub-regions required when the lower boundary changes expression across the y-axis.

interactionPlan.concept: Decomposing double integrals into sub-regions when boundary formulas change, and avoiding decomposition by changing the order of integration.

demo_steps.title: Why Split the Region?
demo_steps.narration: In Type I integration, we slice vertically. Looking from left to right, the lower boundary changes its formula at x = 0 from y = -x + 1 to y = x + 1. This forces us to split the region into R1 and R2.

demo_steps.title: Modify the Boundaries
demo_steps.narration: Try editing the boundary equations. Notice how the blue (R1) and yellow (R2) regions automatically adjust their shapes and limits based on your functions.

demo_steps.title: The Type II Shortcut
demo_steps.narration: Switch to Type II (horizontal) integration. By slicing horizontally, the left boundary is always x = -(y - 1) and the right boundary is always x = y - 1, meaning we only need a single integral!

interactionPlan.keyInsight: If the boundary of an integration region changes analytical formula mid-way, you must split the region into separate double integrals. Choosing the alternative integration order (Type II instead of Type I) often avoids this split entirely.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Create an interactive 2D Cartesian coordinate plane. Show a triangular region bounded by y=3 at the top. The lower left boundary is colored blue, lower right is colored orange. Left subregion R1 is shaded pale blue with a red vertical strip; right subregion R2 is shaded pale yellow with a red vertical strip. When Type II is selected, the vertical split disappears, the entire region merges into one color (pale purple), and a single blue horizontal strip with arrows pointing left/right is shown instead. Render dynamic LaTeX equations below the graph showing the resulting integral setups.

- equation_input for the two lower boundary equations: two fields pre-filled with "-x + 1" (left, for R1) and "x + 1" (right, for R2); when the learner edits either, the corresponding boundary line redraws, the shaded sub-regions R1 and R2 update, and the inner integral limits display — shows directly how the lower boundary formula changing expression at x=0 is what forces the decomposition into two sub-integrals
- toggle between Type I (vertical slices, R1 + R2 split with red strips) and Type II (horizontal slices, single region with blue horizontal strips and limits x from -(y-1) to (y-1)) — teaches that switching integration order eliminates the need to decompose R
